sec.title: Tissue immune cell atlas
sec.p: We next examined the TICA dataset (Domínguez Conde et al., 2022), comprising paired RNA and VDJ profiles of human T cells across tissues and donors. As in previous analyses, TopoMetry identified numerous clusters within the CD4+ compartment that were either merged or absent in both the PCA-based workflow and original cell type annotations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3a–b). Using the scirpy TCR analysis toolkit (Sturm et al., 2020), we queried epitope databases for antigens matching the TCR repertoire of this dataset, and found that the additional clusters uncovered by TopoMetry recognized antigens from specific species (Figure 5—figure supplement 3c). Of note, we found that one of TopoMetry’s clusters corresponded to a single clonotype of tissue-resident memory T CD8+ cells with specificity for SARS-CoV-2 antigens (Figure 5—figure supplement 3c). To further investigate clonal expansion dynamics, we visualized the 30 largest clonotypes with TopoMetry, and found a strong correspondence between these clonotypes and the fine-grained cluster structure identified by TopoMetry (Figure 5—figure supplement 3c). Several of these clusters corresponded to hyperexpanded clones, including the population recognizing SARS-CoV-2 antigens (Figure 5—figure supplement 3e). Clonal expansion analysis further confirmed that hyperexpanded clones mapped to distinct CD8+ and NK populations, whereas the TopoMetry-specific CD4+ clusters corresponded to clonotypes with modest expansion (Figure 5—figure supplement 3f). Finally, to evaluate the specificity of the cluster-clonotype associations between workflows, we performed TCR repertoire overlap analysis, revealing that the PCA-based workflow and original cell type annotations resulted in strong repertoire overlap (Figure 5—figure supplement 3f). The ‘pure’ standalone kNN workflow (Figure 5—figure supplement 3g) presented clearly weaker overlap, followed by TopoMetry (Figure 5—figure supplement 3h), which presented minimal overlap. These results demonstrate that TopoMetry’s clustering results achieve a strong association with clonotypes inferred from TCR sequence similarity, in contrast to the poor performance of the PCA-based approach and the intermediate performance of standalone kNN graphs.

Collectively, these results show that TopoMetry’s geometry-aware workflow uncovers transcriptional imprints of TCR clonotypes directly from RNA expression. Across both SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and atlas-scale datasets, the additional T cell clusters revealed by TopoMetry corresponded to clonally distinct populations, many of which were invisible to PCA-based workflows. This finding closes the loop on our incidental observation in PBMC data: the unexpected T cell diversity resolved by TopoMetry reflects the clonal architecture of the immune repertoire. More broadly, these analyses highlight how preserving geometry enables faithful recovery of biological structure, bridging transcriptional diversity with clonotype identity in a way that linear or density-biased methods fail to achieve.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this work, we introduced TopoMetry, a framework for geometry-aware analysis of single-cell data that systematically learns manifold structure directly from the data. By constructing similarity graphs with kernels adaptive to local density and intrinsic dimensionality, TopoMetry extracts spectral scaffolds that capture the full range of geometric variation present in cellular systems. These scaffolds serve as the basis for refined diffusion graphs that preserve both local neighborhoods and long-range relationships, enabling downstream tasks such as clustering, visualization, imputation, and lineage inference in a way that is faithful to the original geometry. Crucially, TopoMetry also provides operator-native fidelity scores and distortion diagnostics, allowing users to evaluate when and how embeddings diverge from the underlying manifold. Applications across diverse datasets demonstrated that TopoMetry yields stable, faithful, and interpretable representations, often revealing subtle yet biologically meaningful structures invisible to existing workflows. Most notably, TopoMetry uncovered an unexpectedly rich transcriptional landscape of T cells in peripheral blood, linked to TCR repertoires and clonal expansion, demonstrating the biological insights that become accessible when geometry is preserved.

The results presented here also expose fundamental flaws in the current PCA→UMAP standard. The reliance on PCA as a first analysis step imposes restrictive assumptions: that linear variance captures the relevant biological signal and that the dataset is globally well-approximated by a low-rank linear subspace (Pearson, 1901; Jolliffe, 1986). Our systematic evaluation shows that these assumptions fail dramatically in single-cell genomics: PCA typically explains <40% of the variance in standard settings, and the variance explained decreases as the number of highly variable genes (HVGs) grows. These results mean that PCA discards the majority of biological signal before manifold learning even begins. The consequence is clear: PCA-based embeddings systematically collapse diverse cell populations into broad, poorly resolved clusters, as observed with datasets containing T cells, where lineage- and clonotype-associated subpopulations vanish into a single homogeneous cloud. UMAP then compounds the issue by optimizing the layout from the already distorted PCA-based neighborhood graph. The field has relied on this standard for years–not because it is faithful, but because it is convenient. Our results demonstrate that such convenience comes at the cost of accuracy, discarding most of the underlying information and obscuring biologically meaningful structure.

TopoMetry does not simply extend previous diffusion-based methods such as Diffusion Maps (Coifman and Lafon, 2006) or PHATE (Moon et al., 2019); it provides a systematic and general framework for geometric analysis and manifold learning in single-cell data. Diffusion Maps introduced the idea of capturing data geometry across scales, while PHATE emphasized visualization of diffusion potentials. TopoMetry unifies and generalizes these insights into a pipeline that is both rigorous and practical: adaptive kernels ensure robustness to uneven sampling, spectral scaffolds encode manifold structure at data-driven resolutions, refined operators capture ‘the geometry of the geometry,’ geometry preservation metrics evaluate the learned representations, and Riemannian diagnostics offer principled tools for assessing distortion in visualizations. This combination of theory and practice positions TopoMetry as a distinct step forward. Importantly, its impact is already visible in the field: Hale et al. recently used TopoMetry to detect morphologically distinct T cell populations in a high-content imaging study published in Science (Hale et al., 2024), and Tedeschi et al., 2025 integrated it into their analysis of multimodal single-cell atlases. That independent groups are already leveraging TopoMetry underscores its utility and relevance.

As with any method, TopoMetry has limitations. Its current implementation is optimized for exploratory analysis rather than for online mapping of new cells, which restricts its use in scenarios requiring direct projection into precomputed manifolds. Computational cost is another consideration: although scalable to millions of cells, geometric analysis is still more computationally intensive than PCA. Finally, while our discovery of clonally linked T cell populations highlights the method’s ability to reveal new biology, these findings call for follow-up experimental validation. Encouragingly, studies employing joint representations learned from paired TCR and RNA data have identified populations that resemble those identified by TopoMetry (Zhang et al., 2023; Drost et al., 2024), indicating that these arise from reproducible biological signals.

Future work will extend TopoMetry’s geometric-centered vision in several directions. Integrating geometric autoencoders (Duque et al., 2023) could enable inverse mapping and online embedding of new cells. Extensions to multimodal data are natural, particularly for integrating RNA, chromatin, protein, and receptor information into unified geometry-aware representations (Hao et al., 2021). Biologically, TopoMetry opens new opportunities to study T cell clonality, lineage diversification, and other processes where subtle geometric variation encodes key biological signals. More broadly, the framework could be applied to any high-dimensional single-cell modality, from epigenomics to imaging cytometry, wherever faithful preservation of geometry matters.

In sum, TopoMetry represents a conceptual shift: a framework that places geometry at the center of single-cell analysis and a tool for discovery, capable of revealing structure even in datasets that have already been thoroughly examined by the community. The rich T cell diversity uncovered in PBMC data, long considered a ‘solved’ dataset and ubiquitously used for tutorials and demonstrations, illustrates this power. Far from being exhausted, such datasets are valuable resources of potentially new biological insight if analyzed with appropriate geometric tools. TopoMetry provides these tools, and in doing so, it sets the stage for a new generation of geometry-aware single-cell genomics.

sec.title: Manifold hypothesis and sampling model
sec.p: Let M⊂RD\begin{document}$\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D}$\end{document} be a compact, d\begin{document}$d$\end{document}-dimensional C2\begin{document}$C^{2}$\end{document} Riemannian submanifold (possibly with boundary) with metric g\begin{document}$g$\end{document} induced by the ambient Euclidean metric and volume measure dVg\begin{document}$\mathrm{d}V_{g}$\end{document}. We observe points x1,…,xN∈RD\begin{document}$x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$\end{document} drawn i.i.d. from a distribution supported on (or in a tubular neighborhood of) M\begin{document}$\mathcal{M}$\end{document}. In the on-manifold case,xi∼q⁢d⁢Vg,q:ℳ→ℝ≥0⁢unknown (not necessarily uniform).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle x_{i}\sim q\,\mathrm{d}V_{g},\qquad q:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\ \text {unknown (not necessarily uniform)}.$$\end{document}

In the near-manifold case, xi=ξi+εi\begin{document}$x_{i}=\xi_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}$\end{document} with ξi∼qdVg\begin{document}$\xi_{i}\sim q\,\mathrm{d}V_{g}$\end{document} on M\begin{document}$\mathcal{M}$\end{document} and small ambient noise εi\begin{document}$\varepsilon_{i}$\end{document} supported in a tubular neighborhood; when needed we write π(xi)∈M\begin{document}$\pi(x_{i})\in\mathcal{M}$\end{document} for the nearest-point projection and assume π#μ=qdVg\begin{document}$\pi_{\#}\mu=q\,\mathrm{d}V_{g}$\end{document}.

sec.title: Overview
sec.p: We adopt the manifold hypothesis in a form tailored to single-cell data: the observed profiles x1,…,xN∈RD\begin{document}$x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$\end{document} are sampled on (or very near) a d\begin{document}$d$\end{document}-dimensional Riemannian submanifold M⊂RD\begin{document}$\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D}$\end{document} according to an unknown, not-necessarily uniform sampling density q\begin{document}$q$\end{document} with respect to the manifold’s volume measure. Our goal is to recover informative, low-distortion coordinates that reflect the intrinsic geometry of M\begin{document}$\mathcal{M}$\end{document} rather than artifacts of the ambient space.

A principled way to expose this geometry is via the Laplace–Beltrami operator (LBO), Δg\begin{document}$\Delta_{g}$\end{document}, the natural generalization of the Laplacian to curved spaces. Its eigenfunctions act like a ‘Fourier basis’ on M\begin{document}$\mathcal{M}$\end{document}: low-frequency eigenfunctions capture broad organization, while higher frequencies resolve finer structure. In practice, Δg\begin{document}$\Delta_{g}$\end{document} is not observed directly; instead, methods such as (Belkin and Niyogi, 2003; Coifman and Lafon, 2006) build a graph Laplacian from an affinity (similarity) graph on the samples. This graph operator converges to Δg\begin{document}$\Delta_{g}$\end{document}, especially when affinities are computed with manifold-adaptive kernels that correct for nonuniform sampling q\begin{document}$q$\end{document} (Berry and Harlim, 2016).

TopoMetry builds on this theory by constructing a spectral scaffold: an orthonormal eigenbasis of graph-LBO eigenvectors that provides data-driven, intrinsic coordinates. Each eigenvector can be read as a smooth ‘mode of variation’ across cells, and the collection of the leading modes spans a coordinate system that encodes both local neighborhoods and global relationships. To avoid choosing a single resolution, TopoMetry forms a multiscale spectral scaffold by reweighting these modes across diffusion times (powers of the diffusion operator), thereby blending fine-grained and long-range structure in a single representation. The scaffold size is automatically selected from intrinsic-dimensionality estimates, so that subtle transcriptional signals and broad phenotypic organization are both retained without ad hoc parameter tuning.

Finally, TopoMetry reconstructs a neighborhood graph in the scaffold space and learns the corresponding graph LBO of the spectral scaffold itself—capturing the ‘geometry of the geometry’. The resulting operators (diffusion potentials and refined similarity graphs) serve as high-fidelity inputs for downstream analyses such as clustering, trajectory inference, pseudotime, and layout optimization (e.g. MAP, PaCMAP). In short, TopoMetry progressively denoises and sharpens manifold structure across scales, yielding coordinates that are stable, interpretable, and faithful to the intrinsic geometry of single-cell atlases.

sec.title: Computational implementation
sec.p: TopoMetry was designed for ease of use and computational efficiency. It integrates popular approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) libraries such as NMSlib and hnswlib. Most graph operations are performed on sparse matrices and scale efficiently with multithreading. Each workflow step is implemented as a modular scikit-learn-style transformer, enabling custom pipelines. Core modules include estimators of neighborhood graphs, affinity kernels and operators, eigendecompositions, and layout optimizations. Analyses are orchestrated by the TopOGraph class. The modular design allows seamless integration with machine-learning and single-cell analysis pipelines. Additional utilities estimate intrinsic dimensionalities, evaluate embeddings, and visualize results. High-level APIs simplify usage: a single line of code can run a complete analysis and output a comprehensive report, including direct compatibility with Scanpy (Wolf et al., 2018) and the broader Python ecosystem for single-cell analyses. The source code is available at https://github.com/davisidarta/topometry (copy archived at Sidarta-Oliveira, 2026). Documentation and tutorials are available at https://topometry.readthedocs.io/en/latest/.

sec.title: Assumed input
sec.p: TopoMetry expects as input a cell-by-feature matrix that has been scaled or standardized, typically by Z-score normalization of gene expression. This preprocessing ensures that each feature contributes comparably to similarity calculations and avoids dominance by highly expressed or variable genes. A standardized input is also advantageous because it allows cell–cell similarity to be computed directly from feature correlations. In practice, this is implemented efficiently using cosine distances, which are equivalent to correlation distances on standardized data. In single-cell genomics, the input is usually subset to include only highly variable features, and we employed such standard preprocessing with default parameters in all demonstrated analyses.

sec.title: Distance calculation
sec.p: Distances are computed differently at each stage of the workflow. For building the initial spectral scaffold, we use cosine distance on normalized data, which is robust to differences in sequencing depth and scale and corresponds to the correlation distance when the input is standardized. The cosine (or correlation) distance between two cells xi,xj∈Rd\begin{document}$x_{i},x_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$\end{document} is defined as:dcos⁢(xi,xj)= 1-⟨xi,xj⟩∥xi∥2⁢∥xj∥2,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle d_{\cos}(x_{i},x_{j})\;=\;1-\frac{\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle}{\|x_{i}\|_{2}\, \|x_{j}\|_{2}},$$\end{document}
where 〈·,·〉 denotes the Euclidean inner product.

For refined graphs built on the scaffold (Pof\_Z\begin{document}$P_{\text{of\_Z}}$\end{document}), we use Euclidean distance in the learned spectral coordinates, which provides a natural metric for diffusion geometry. The Euclidean distance between two spectral embeddings zi,zj∈Rr\begin{document}$z_{i},z_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$\end{document} is defined as:dEuc⁢(zi,zj)=∑k=1r(zi⁢k-zj⁢k)2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{Euc}}(z_{i},z_{j})\;=\;\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{r}\bigl{(}z_{ik}-z_{jk} \bigr{)}^{2}}.$$\end{document}

sec.title: Kernels and affinity estimation
sec.p: Let M⊂RM\begin{document}$\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{M}$\end{document} be (near) a Riemannian submanifold with unknown sampling density q\begin{document}$q$\end{document}. For each sample xi∈RM\begin{document}$x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}$\end{document}, denote by nbrs(xi)\begin{document}$\mathrm{nbrs}(x_{i})$\end{document} the ordered set of its k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}-nearest neighbors under a chosen dissimilarity d(⋅,⋅)\begin{document}$d(\cdot,\cdot)$\end{document} (Euclidean or cosine-based; see ‘Cosine/correlation geometry’ below). The affinity graph W∈R≥0N×N\begin{document}$W\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N\times N}$\end{document} is built from locally rescaled distances and then symmetrized.

sec.title: Adaptive scaling (per-point bandwidth)
sec.p: For robustness to heterogeneous sampling, a local bandwidth σi\begin{document}$\sigma_{i}$\end{document} is estimated from the median neighbor distance of xi\begin{document}$x_{i}$\end{document}:σi=d⁢(xi,nbrs(m)⁢(xi)),m=⌊k2⌋,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma_{i}\;=\;d\!\left(x_{i},\,\mathrm{nbrs}_{(m)}(x_{i})\right),\qquad m= \Big{\lfloor}\frac{k}{2}\Big{\rfloor},$$\end{document}

that is the m\begin{document}$m$\end{document}-th order statistic of {d(xi,xj):xj∈nbrs(xi)}\begin{document}$\{d(x_{i},x_{j}):x_{j}\in\mathrm{nbrs}(x_{i})\}$\end{document}. This σi\begin{document}$\sigma_{i}$\end{document} encodes local crowding (small in dense regions, large in sparse ones) and stabilizes locality.

sec.title: Cosine/correlation geometry and angularization
sec.p: When using the cosine metric, we convert cosine distance dijcos=1−cos⁡∠(xi,xj)∈[0,2]\begin{document}$d^{\cos}_{ij}=1-\cos\angle(x_{i},x_{j})\in[0,2]$\end{document} to an angle θij∈[0,π]\begin{document}$\theta_{ij}\in[0,\pi]$\end{document},θi⁢j=arccos⁡(1-di⁢jcos)=arccos⁡(⟨xi,xj⟩∥xi∥2⁢∥xj∥2),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \theta_{ij}\;=\;\arccos\!\big{(}1-d^{\cos}_{ij}\big{)}\;=\;\arccos\!\Big{(} \tfrac{\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle}{\|x_{i}\|_{2}\,\|x_{j}\|_{2}}\Big{)},$$\end{document}

and use dij:=θij\begin{document}$d_{ij}:=\theta_{ij}$\end{document} instead of the Euclidean distance. On feature-wise standardized (z-scored) inputs, cos⁡∠(xi,xj)\begin{document}$\cos\angle(x_{i},x_{j})$\end{document} equals the Pearson correlation, so θij=arccos⁡(ρij)\begin{document}$\theta_{ij}=\arccos(\rho_{ij})$\end{document} places similarities on the unit sphere (‘correlation geometry’). Distances are numerically clipped to their natural ranges [0,π]\begin{document}$[0,\pi]$\end{document} (angular) or [0, 2] (cosine), and optionally squared (default), before kernelization.

sec.title: Bandwidth-adaptive (variable) kernel
sec.p: We first form a left-normalized, variable-bandwidth dissimilarityd~i⁢j=di⁢jσi+ε,ε>0⁢ small,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \widetilde{d}_{ij}\;=\;\frac{d_{ij}}{\sigma_{i}+\varepsilon},\qquad\varepsilon \gt 0\text{ small,}$$\end{document}

which rescales each row by its local scale σi\begin{document}$\sigma_{i}$\end{document}. The basic affinity is thenWi⁢j(vb)=exp⁡(-d~i⁢jp),p=2⁢by default (square distances).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle W_{ij}^{(\text{vb})}\;=\;\exp\!\big{(}-\,\widetilde{d}_{ij}^{\,p}\big{)}, \qquad p=2\ \text{by default (square distances).}$$\end{document}

Finally, we symmetrize W←(W+W⊤)/2\begin{document}$W\leftarrow(W+W^{\top})/2$\end{document}. This row-wise scaling followed by symmetrization closely approximates classical (σi,σj)\begin{document}$(\sigma_{i},\sigma_{j})$\end{document}-variable bandwidth kernels while being simple and fast to compute.

sec.title: Neighborhood density and ‘pseudomedian’
sec.p: From {σi}i=1N\begin{document}$\{\sigma_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$\end{document} we derive a continuous density proxy ωi\begin{document}$\omega_{i}$\end{document} by linearly mapping the interval [minjσj,maxjσj]\begin{document}$[\min_{j}\sigma_{j},\max_{j}\sigma_{j}]$\end{document} to [2,k]\begin{document}$[2,k]$\end{document}:ωi=linmap⁢(σi;[min⁡σ,max⁡σ]→[2,k]).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \omega_{i}\;=\;\mathrm{linmap}\!\Big{(}\sigma_{i};\,[\min\sigma,\max\sigma]\to [2,k]\Big{)}.$$\end{document}

Large ωi\begin{document}$\omega_{i}$\end{document} (near k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}) indicates sparsity; small ωi\begin{document}$\omega_{i}$\end{document} (near 2) indicates locality within dense regions. This quantity can guide mild neighbor-set expansion in under-sampled areas (optionally replacing k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} with k′≥k\begin{document}$k^{\prime}\geq k$\end{document}) and parameterizes the adaptive decaying kernel.

sec.title: Adaptively decaying kernel (density-dependent tails)
sec.p: To slow decay in sparse regions and sharpen it in dense ones, we make the decay exponent a function of ωi\begin{document}$\omega_{i}$\end{document}. Defineηi= 2k-ωiωi∈[1,∞),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \eta_{i}\;=\;2^{\frac{k-\omega_{i}}{\omega_{i}}}\in[1,\infty),$$\end{document}

so that ηi≈1\begin{document}$\eta_{i}\approx 1$\end{document} in sparse areas (ωi≈k\begin{document}$\omega_{i}\approx k$\end{document}) and ηi\begin{document}$\eta_{i}$\end{document} grows as neighborhoods become denser. Using the same left-normalized d~ij\begin{document}$\widetilde{d}_{ij}$\end{document}, we setWi⁢j(ad)=exp⁡(-d~i⁢jpi),pi={2(standard, no adaptive decay),2⁢ηi(adaptive decay with squared distances).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle W_{ij}^{(\text{ad})}\;=\;\exp\!\Big{(}-\,\widetilde{d}_{ij}^{\,p_{i}}\Big{)}, \qquad p_{i}\;=\;\begin{cases}2&\text{(standard, no adaptive decay)},\\[2.0pt] 2\,\eta_{i}&\text{(adaptive decay with squared distances).}\end{cases}$$\end{document}

Equivalently, with squared distances disabled, one uses pi=ηi\begin{document}$p_{i}=\eta_{i}$\end{document}. The resulting kernel decays gently across sparse regions (preserving informative long-range neighbors) and more steeply inside dense regions (preventing oversmoothing). As above, we symmetrize W\begin{document}$W$\end{document} at the end.

sec.title: Fixed-bandwidth (global) kernel
sec.p: For comparison or when desired, a global scale σ>0\begin{document}$\sigma \gt 0$\end{document} yieldsWi⁢j(fb)=exp⁡(-(di⁢j/σ)p),p=2⁢by default.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle W_{ij}^{(\text{fb})}\;=\;\exp\!\Big{(}-\,(d_{ij}/\sigma)^{p}\Big{)},\qquad p=2 \ \text{by default.}$$\end{document}

sec.title: Summary
sec.p: TopoMetry provides: (i) a fixed-bandwidth Gaussian/RBF kernel; (ii) a variable, per-point bandwidth kernel using median-k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} scaling; (iii) an optional neighborhood-expansion variant driven by the density proxy ωi\begin{document}$\omega_{i}$\end{document}; and (iv) an adaptively decaying kernel with density-dependent exponents. Distance preprocessing supports Euclidean geometry and correlation/cosine geometry via angularization. These design choices make affinity estimation sensitive to manifold structure while robust to heterogeneous sampling, providing a stable foundation for subsequent Laplace–Beltrami operator approximations and diffusion-based embeddings.

sec.title: Intrinsic dimensionality estimation
sec.p: Intrinsic dimensionality (i.d.) can be loosely defined as the minimum number of parameters needed to describe a high-dimensional system accurately. Multiple notions exist (e.g. local vs. global i.d.), and accurate estimation remains an active area of research. Estimating the global i.d. of a dataset is closely related to estimating the dimensionality of its underlying manifold, which is crucial when selecting the number of components for dimensionality reduction. Local i.d. is also useful as an auxiliary variable to characterize data geometry. Notably, the similarity kernels employed in TopoMetry are related to the Farahmand–Szepesvári–Audibert (FSA) estimator, leveraging ratios of distances to the k/2\begin{document}$k/2$\end{document}- and k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}-th nearest neighbors as a proxy for local sampling density.

sec.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE)
sec.p: Consider i.i.d. observations Xi=g(Yi)\begin{document}$X_{i}=g(Y_{i})$\end{document} that embed lower-dimensional samples Yi\begin{document}$Y_{i}$\end{document} drawn from an unknown density f\begin{document}$f$\end{document} via a continuous, smooth map g\begin{document}$g$\end{document}. For a point x\begin{document}$x$\end{document}, assume f(x)\begin{document}$f(x)$\end{document} is approximately constant within a small sphere Sx(R)\begin{document}$S_{x}(R)$\end{document} of radius R\begin{document}$R$\end{document}, so observations in Sx(R)\begin{document}$S_{x}(R)$\end{document} form a homogeneous Poisson process. Replacing the radius by the k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}-nearest neighbors yields the local MLE for intrinsic dimension around x\begin{document}$x$\end{document}:m^k⁢(x)=[1k-1⁢∑j=1k-1log⁡Tk⁢(x)Tj⁢(x)]-1,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat{m}_{k}(x)\;=\;\bigg{[}\frac{1}{k-1}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\log\!\frac{T_{k}(x)}{ T_{j}(x)}\bigg{]}^{-1},$$\end{document}

where Tj(x)\begin{document}$T_{j}(x)$\end{document} is the distance from x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} to its j\begin{document}$j$\end{document}-th nearest neighbor. A global estimate is obtained by averaging the local estimates over all x\begin{document}$x$\end{document}.

sec.title: Manifold-adaptive dimensionality estimation (FSA)
sec.p: The FSA method uses two nested neighborhoods around x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} (at k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} and k/2\begin{document}$k/2$\end{document} neighbors) to estimate local i.d.:δk⁢(x)=log⁡2log⁡(Rk⁢(x)/Rk/2⁢(x)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \delta_{k}(x)\;=\;\frac{\log 2}{\log\!\big{(}R_{k}(x)/R_{k/2}(x)\big{)}},$$\end{document}

where Rj(x)\begin{document}$R_{j}(x)$\end{document} denotes the distance from x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} to its j\begin{document}$j$\end{document}-th nearest neighbor. The ratio Rk/Rk/2\begin{document}$R_{k}/R_{k/2}$\end{document} coincides with the scaling factor used in TopoMetry’s bandwidth-adaptive kernel. The global i.d. is reported as the median of the local δk(x)\begin{document}$\delta_{k}(x)$\end{document} values.

sec.title: Laplacian-type and diffusion operators
sec.p: Let W∈R≥0N×N\begin{document}$W\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N\times N}$\end{document} be a symmetric affinity (similarity) matrix built on the samples, with zero diagonal. Denote the (weighted) degree of node i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} by di=∑jWij\begin{document}$d_{i}=\sum_{j}W_{ij}$\end{document} and D=diag(d1,…,dN)\begin{document}$D=\mathrm{diag}(d_{1},\dots,d_{N})$\end{document}. Graph Laplacians translate this similarity structure into linear operators whose spectra summarize geometry and connectivity; diffusion operators turn W\begin{document}$W$\end{document} into a Markov process on cells.

Three standard graph Laplacians:(i) Unnormalized: L=D-W.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{(i) Unnormalized:}\quad L\;=\;D-W.$$\end{document}(ii) Symmetric normalized: Lsym=D-1/2⁢L⁢D-1/2=I-D-1/2⁢W⁢D-1/2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{(ii) Symmetric normalized:}\quad L_{\mathrm{sym}}\;=\;D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2} \;=\;I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}.$$\end{document}(iii) Random-walk (row-normalized): Lrw=D-1⁢L=I-D-1⁢W.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{(iii) Random-walk (row-normalized):}\quad L_{\mathrm{rw}}\;=\;D^{-1}L\;= \;I-D^{-1}W.$$\end{document}

All three are positive semidefinite on a connected graph, with a trivial eigenpair (0,1)\begin{document}$(0,\mathbf{1})$\end{document}. In practice, Lsym\begin{document}$L_{\mathrm{sym}}$\end{document} is convenient for symmetric eigensolvers and is less sensitive to degree heterogeneity; Lrw\begin{document}$L_{\mathrm{rw}}$\end{document} is directly linked to random walks and diffusion. Spectral embeddings such as Laplacian Eigenmaps (Belkin and Niyogi, 2003) use the eigenvectors associated with the smallest nonzero eigenvalues of one of these Laplacians (often dropping the constant eigenvector) as intrinsic coordinates.

sec.title: Diffusion operator and diffusion time
sec.p: Row-normalizing W\begin{document}$W$\end{document} yields the (row-stochastic) diffusion operatorP=D-1⁢W,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle P\;=\;D^{-1}W,$$\end{document}

which defines a Markov chain on cells: (Pt)ij\begin{document}$(P^{t})_{ij}$\end{document} is the probability of transitioning from cell i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} to cell j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} in t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} steps. The leading eigenvalues λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥0\begin{document}$\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 0$\end{document} and right eigenvectors ψ1,ψ2,…\begin{document}$\psi_{1},\psi_{2},\dots$\end{document} of P\begin{document}$P$\end{document} provide diffusion coordinates at time t\begin{document}$t$\end{document},Ψt⁢(i)=(λ1t⁢ψ1⁢(i),λ2t⁢ψ2⁢(i),…),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Psi_{t}(i)\;=\;\big{(}\lambda_{1}^{\,t}\psi_{1}(i),\,\lambda_{2}^{\,t}\psi_{2 }(i),\,\ldots\big{)},$$\end{document}

which emphasize multi-step connectivity and progressively suppress noise (Coifman and Lafon, 2006). When a single t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} is not desired, one can use alternative scalings (e.g., ‘diffusion potential’ mappings) that highlight long-range structure without fixing t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}.

sec.title: Anisotropic (α) normalization to reduce sampling bias
sec.p: Nonuniform sampling density can bias graph operators. A standard correction (Diffusion Maps) reweights W\begin{document}$W$\end{document} by powers of the degree before row-normalization:W(α)=D-α⁢W⁢D-α,Dα=diag⁢(W(α)⁢𝟏),P(α)=Dα-1⁢W(α).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle W^{(\alpha)}\;=\;D^{-\alpha}\,W\,D^{-\alpha},\qquad D_{\alpha}\;=\;\mathrm{ diag}\big{(}W^{(\alpha)}\mathbf{1}\big{)},\qquad P^{(\alpha)}\;=\;D_{\alpha}^{ -1}\,W^{(\alpha)}.$$\end{document}

Here 0≤α≤1\begin{document}$0\leq\alpha\leq 1$\end{document} tunes the level of debiasing: α=0\begin{document}$\alpha=0$\end{document} leaves W\begin{document}$W$\end{document} unchanged; α=1\begin{document}$\alpha=1$\end{document} largely removes effects of sampling density. A related ‘semi-anisotropic’ variant applies the degree correction during normalization while retaining the original edge weights W\begin{document}$W$\end{document}; this can stabilize spectra while preserving the original notion of similarity.

sec.title: Symmetric diffusion operator for stable spectra
sec.p: While P(α)\begin{document}$P^{(\alpha)}$\end{document} is generally asymmetric, it is similar to a symmetric matrix with the same eigenvalues:Psym(α)=Dα-1/2⁢W(α)⁢Dα-1/2=Dα1/2⁢P(α)⁢Dα-1/2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(\alpha)}\;=\;D_{\alpha}^{-1/2}\,W^{(\alpha)}\,D_{\alpha}^{- 1/2}\;=\;D_{\alpha}^{1/2}\,P^{(\alpha)}\,D_{\alpha}^{-1/2}.$$\end{document}

This Hermitian form is numerically well behaved; its eigenvectors can be mapped back to those of P(α)\begin{document}$P^{(\alpha)}$\end{document} by left-multiplication with Dα−1/2\begin{document}$D_{\alpha}^{-1/2}$\end{document}. Diffusion-map embeddings are then obtained from the leading eigenpairs of P(α)\begin{document}$P^{(\alpha)}$\end{document} (or equivalently Psym(α)\begin{document}$P_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(\alpha)}$\end{document}), optionally raised to diffusion time t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}.

sec.title: Connections to manifold geometry
sec.p: Under standard assumptions (smooth manifold, appropriate kernels and bandwidths), graph Laplacians converge to the Laplace–Beltrami operator Δg\begin{document}$\Delta_{g}$\end{document} on the data manifold, and Pt\begin{document}$P^{t}$\end{document} approximates heat diffusion etΔg\begin{document}$e^{t\Delta_{g}}$\end{document} (Belkin and Niyogi, 2003; Coifman and Lafon, 2006). This link justifies using Laplacian- and diffusion-based spectra as intrinsic, geometry-aware coordinates for downstream single-cell analysis.

sec.title: Eigendecomposition, spectral scaffolds, and multiscaling
sec.p: Let P∈RN×N\begin{document}$P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$\end{document} be the diffusion operator derived from the affinity graph. We start from the eigendecompositionP⁢ψℓ=λℓ⁢ψℓ,ℓ=1,2,…,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle P\,\psi_{\ell}\;=\;\lambda_{\ell}\,\psi_{\ell},\qquad\ell=1,2,\dots,$$\end{document}

with eigenvalues ordered by magnitude 1=λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥0\begin{document}$1=\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 0$\end{document}. For numerical stability it is often convenient to work with a symmetric similarity Psym=D1/2PD−1/2\begin{document}$P_{\mathrm{sym}}=D^{1/2}PD^{-1/2}$\end{document}, which is similar to P\begin{document}$P$\end{document} and therefore has the same spectrum; its eigenvectors are orthonormal in the Euclidean inner product and can be mapped back to right–eigenvectors of P\begin{document}$P$\end{document} by left multiplication with D−1/2\begin{document}$D^{-1/2}$\end{document}.

sec.title: Spectral scaffold
sec.p: We define the spectral scaffold asΨ=[ψ1,ψ2,…,ψr]∈ℝN×r,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Psi\;=\;[\,\psi_{1},\;\psi_{2},\;\ldots,\;\psi_{r}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r},$$\end{document}

whose columns are mutually orthogonal (orthonormal after normalization) and ordered by decreasing |λℓ|\begin{document}$|\lambda_{\ell}|$\end{document}. The leading column ψ1\begin{document}$\psi_{1}$\end{document} is the trivial stationary mode (constant on each connected component) and is dropped in embeddings. The scaffold size r\begin{document}$r$\end{document} is chosen adaptively using intrinsic dimensionality estimates and eigengap heuristics, so it expands or contracts with dataset complexity rather than being fixed a priori.

sec.title: Diffusion coordinates at timescale t
sec.p: Geometry at a specific diffusion timescale t∈N\begin{document}$t\in\mathbb{N}$\end{document} is obtained by reweighting scaffold columns by λℓt\begin{document}$\lambda_{\ell}^{\,t}$\end{document}. For cell i,Φt(i)=(λ1tψ1(i),λ2tψ2(i),…,λrtψr(i))=Ψ(i,⋅)diag⁡(λ1t,…,λrt),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Phi_{t}(i) = \left( \lambda_{1}^{\,t}\psi_{1}(i), \lambda_{2}^{\,t}\psi_{2}(i), \ldots, \lambda_{r}^{\,t}\psi_{r}(i) \right) = \Psi(i,\cdot)\, \operatorname{diag} \left( \lambda_{1}^{\,t}, \ldots, \lambda_{r}^{\,t} \right),$$\end{document}
which progressively suppresses high-frequency (noise-like) components as t increases, emphasizing long-range organization.

sec.title: Multiscale spectral scaffold
sec.p: Besides using single t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}, TopoMetry builds a multiscale representation by analytically aggregating all diffusion times. Using the geometric-series identity ∑t=1∞λℓt=λℓ/(1−λℓ)\begin{document}$\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}^{t}=\lambda_{\ell}/(1-\lambda_{\ell})$\end{document} (valid for λℓ∈[0,1)\begin{document}$\lambda_{\ell}\in[0,1)$\end{document} and after removing the trivial mode λ1=1\begin{document}$\lambda_{1}=1$\end{document}, we formΦms⁢(i)=(λ21-λ2⁢ψ2⁢(i),λ31-λ3⁢ψ3⁢(i),…,λr1-λr⁢ψr⁢(i)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Phi_{\mathrm{ms}}(i)\;=\;\bigg{(}\,\frac{\lambda_{2}}{1-\lambda_{2}}\,\psi_{2 }(i),\;\frac{\lambda_{3}}{1-\lambda_{3}}\,\psi_{3}(i),\;\ldots,\;\frac{\lambda _{r}}{1-\lambda_{r}}\,\psi_{r}(i)\bigg{)},$$\end{document}

or, in matrix form,Φms=Ψ⁢diag⁢(λ21-λ2,…,λr1-λr),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Phi_{\mathrm{ms}}\;=\;\Psi\;\mathrm{diag}\!\Big{(}\tfrac{\lambda_{2}}{1- \lambda_{2}},\ldots,\tfrac{\lambda_{r}}{1-\lambda_{r}}\Big{)},$$\end{document}

optionally restricting to eigenvalues λℓ>0\begin{document}$\lambda_{\ell} \gt 0$\end{document} to avoid numerical instabilities. This multiscale spectral scaffold is equivalent to concatenating diffusion coordinates across all times with exponentially decaying weights, thereby blending fine-grained neighborhoods (small t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}) and long-range connectivity (large t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}) in a single, compact set of coordinates.

sec.title: Normalization and symmetry handling
sec.p: When a symmetric similarity is used for eigensolving, the obtained eigenvectors are mapped to the right–eigenvectors of P\begin{document}$P$\end{document} via the similarity transform described above and then ℓ2\begin{document}$\ell_{2}$\end{document}-normalized, ensuring that columns of Ψ\begin{document}$\Psi$\end{document} remain mutually orthogonal. With r\begin{document}$r$\end{document} selected adaptively, the resulting spectral scaffold (single–time Φt\begin{document}$\Phi_{t}$\end{document} or multiscale Φms\begin{document}$\Phi_{\mathrm{ms}}$\end{document}) provides geometry-aware coordinates that adjust to the intrinsic complexity of the single-cell atlas.

sec.title: Refined graph
sec.p: Given spectral coordinates Z∈RN×r\begin{document}$Z\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r}$\end{document} (either a single-time Φt\begin{document}$\Phi_{t}$\end{document} or the multiscale spectral scaffold Φms\begin{document}$\Phi_{\mathrm{ms}}$\end{document}), we rebuild an affinity graph W~\begin{document}$\widetilde{W}$\end{document} in scaffold space to sharpen geometry and suppress residual noise.

sec.title: Construction in Z-space
sec.p: We measure distances with the Euclidean metric dij=‖zi−zj‖2\begin{document}$d_{ij}=\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|_{2}$\end{document}. Using the same adaptive-bandwidth principle as above, each node i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} receives a local scale σi\begin{document}$\sigma_{i}$\end{document} given by the distance to its median k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}-nearest neighbor in Z\begin{document}$Z$\end{document}-space. Affinities are then computed byW~i⁢j=exp⁡(-(di⁢jσi)pi),pi∈{ 2, 2⁢ηi},\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \widetilde{W}_{ij}\;=\;\exp\!\Big{(}-\,\big{(}\tfrac{d_{ij}}{\sigma_{i}}\big{) }^{\,p_{i}}\Big{)},\qquad p_{i}\in\{\,2,\;2\,\eta_{i}\,\},$$\end{document}

where pi=2\begin{document}$p_{i}=2$\end{document} yields a bandwidth-adaptive Gaussian and pi=2ηi\begin{document}$p_{i}=2\,\eta_{i}$\end{document} is an adaptively decaying variant that slows decay in sparse regions and sharpens it in dense ones. The density proxy ωi\begin{document}$\omega_{i}$\end{document} and decay factor ηi=2(k−ωi)/ωi\begin{document}$\eta_{i}=2^{(k-\omega_{i})/\omega_{i}}$\end{document} are defined as in the kernel section. Finally, we symmetrizeW~←12⁢(W~+W~⊤),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \widetilde{W}\;\leftarrow\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\big{(}\widetilde{W}+\widetilde{W}^{ \top}\big{)},$$\end{document}
ensuring a real symmetric affinity suitable for spectral operators (with standard numerical guards).

sec.title: Optional neighborhood expansion
sec.p: In severely under-sampled areas, we allow a mild, density-aware increase of the neighbor set to k′≥k\begin{document}$k^{\prime}\!\geq k$\end{document} (guided by ωi\begin{document}$\omega_{i}$\end{document}), recompute σi\begin{document}$\sigma_{i}$\end{document} on nbrsk′(i)\begin{document}$\mathrm{nbrs}_{k^{\prime}}(i)$\end{document}, and apply the same formulae.

From W~\begin{document}$\widetilde{W}$\end{document} we compute the degree matrix D~=diag(W~1)\begin{document}$\widetilde{D}=\mathrm{diag}(\widetilde{W}\mathbf{1})$\end{document} and derive Laplacian-type operators whose normalization yields refined diffusion operators. By default, TopoMetry applies anisotropic reweighting to these operators, producing a geometry-adapted transition matrix that serves as the backbone for downstream analyses. This refined diffusion operator is then used for tasks such as clustering, trajectory inference, pseudotime analysis, and visualization with graph layout algorithms, ensuring that all inferences are grounded in a refined representation of the original manifold of cell identities.

sec.title: Layout optimization
sec.p: For visualization, TopoMetry applies graph-layout optimization algorithms to the refined graphs. By default, we provide TopoMAP (an efficient UMAP-style layout applied to a precomputed manifold graph) and TopoPaCMAP; both are optimized on the refined diffusion operator and its neighborhood structure. Layout trajectories can be inspected to assess convergence and stability.

sec.title: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)/Manifold Approximation and Projection (MAP)
sec.p: In TopoMetry, MAP denotes applying the same objective to an arbitrary, precomputed manifold graph (here, the refined graph in scaffold space); we refer to this implementation as TopoMAP.

sec.title: Pairwise Controlled Manifold Approximation and Projection (PaCMAP)
sec.p: PaCMAP optimizes a robust pairwise objective that balances three types of pair relationships: (i) near pairs (local neighbors), (ii) mid-near pairs (pairs connecting adjacent neighborhoods), and (iii) further pairs (distant non-neighbors). Let local scales be defined from the average distance to the 4th–6th nearest neighbors; write the high-dimensional, scale-adjusted distance asdi⁢j2=∥xi-xj∥22σi⁢j,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle d^{2}_{ij}\;=\;\frac{\|x_{i}-x_{j}\|_{2}^{2}}{\sigma_{ij}},$$\end{document}

and let dab′=‖ya−yb‖22+1\begin{document}$d^{\prime}_{ab}=\|y_{a}-y_{b}\|_{2}^{2}+1$\end{document} denote the corresponding low-dimensional distance surrogate. The PaCMAP loss isℒPaCMAP=(wnb⁢∑(i,j)∈𝒩di⁢j′10+di⁢j′)+(wmn⁢∑(i,k)∈ℳdi⁢k′104+di⁢k′)+(wfp⁢∑(i,ℓ)∈ℱ110+di⁢ℓ′),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PaCMAP}}\;=\;\Big{(}w_{\mathrm{nb}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal {N}}\frac{d^{\prime}_{ij}}{10+d^{\prime}_{ij}}\Big{)}\;+\;\Big{(}w_{\mathrm{mn }}\sum_{(i,k)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{d^{\prime}_{ik}}{10^{4}+d^{\prime}_{ik}}\Big {)}\;+\;\Big{(}w_{\mathrm{fp}}\sum_{(i,\ell)\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{1}{10+d^{ \prime}_{i\ell}}\Big{)},$$\end{document}

where N,M,F\begin{document}$\mathcal{N},\mathcal{M},\mathcal{F}$\end{document} are the sets of near, mid-near, and further pairs selected per the original sampling rules, and (wnb,wmn,wfp)\begin{document}$(w_{\mathrm{nb}},w_{\mathrm{mn}},w_{\mathrm{fp}})$\end{document} are stage-specific weights (e.g. Stage 1: (2, 1000, 1), Stage 2: (3, 3, 1), Stage 3: (1, 0, 1)). In TopoMetry, PaCMAP is initialized from the spectral scaffold and uses neighbor information from the refined manifold graph, yielding stable, high-fidelity layouts that respect both local neighborhoods and broader organization.

sec.title: Riemann diagnostics and visualizations
sec.p: Let Y∈RN×m\begin{document}$Y\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$\end{document} be an embedding (typically m=2\begin{document}$m=2$\end{document} for visualization) with coordinate functions y(a):{1,…,N}→R\begin{document}$y^{(a)}:\{1,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{R}$\end{document} given by the a\begin{document}$a$\end{document}-th column of Y\begin{document}$Y$\end{document}, and let L∈RN×N\begin{document}$L\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$\end{document} be a (symmetrized) graph Laplacian built on the refined affinity. We center the embedding, Y←Y−1Y¯\begin{document}$Y\leftarrow Y-\mathbf{1}\,\overline{Y}$\end{document}, and write Ly\begin{document}$Ly$\end{document} for the discrete application of L\begin{document}$L$\end{document} to a vector y\begin{document}$y$\end{document}.

sec.title: Discrete dual metric and embedding-space metric
sec.p: For each sample i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and coordinate indices a,b∈{1,…,m}\begin{document}$a,b\in\{1,\dots,m\}$\end{document}, define the discrete dual metric (a covariant tensor) byHa⁢b⁢(i)=12⁢[(L⁢(y(a)⁢y(b)))i-yi(b)⁢(L⁢y(a))i-yi(a)⁢(L⁢y(b))i].\begin{document}$$\displaystyle H_{ab}(i)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\Big{[}(L\,(y^{(a)}y^{(b)}))_{i}\;-\;y^{(b)}_{i}\,(Ly^{(a)})_{i}\;-\;y^{(a)}_{i}\,(Ly^{(b)})_{i}\Big{]}.$$\end{document}

Stacking over a,b\begin{document}$a,b$\end{document} yields H(i)∈Rm×m\begin{document}$H(i)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$\end{document}. We obtain the embedding-space Riemannian metric G(i)\begin{document}$G(i)$\end{document} as the (regularized) pseudoinverse of H(i)\begin{document}$H(i)$\end{document}:H⁢(i)=Ui⁢Si⁢Vi⊤,G⁢(i)=Vi⁢Si†⁢Ui⊤,Si†=diag⁢(1/(si⁢ℓ+ε)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle H(i)\;=\;U_{i}\,S_{i}\,V_{i}^{\top},\qquad G(i)\;=\;V_{i}\,S_{i}^{\dagger}\,U_ {i}^{\top},\qquad S_{i}^{\dagger}=\mathrm{diag}\big{(}1/(s_{i\ell}+\varepsilon)\big{)},$$\end{document}

with a small ε>0\begin{document}$\varepsilon \gt 0$\end{document} to stabilize near-zero singular values. Finally, we project G(i)\begin{document}$G(i)$\end{document} to the symmetric positive definite cone by eigenvalue clipping and normalize its overall scale (e.g. unit trace) to make ellipse sizes comparable across points.

sec.title: Local distortion indicatrix
sec.p: Let G(i)=QiΛiQi⊤\begin{document}$G(i)=Q_{i}\,\Lambda_{i}\,Q_{i}^{\top}$\end{document} with Λi=diag(λi,1≥⋯≥λi,m>0)\begin{document}$\Lambda_{i}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{i,1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{i,m} \gt 0)$\end{document}. The indicatrix at i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} is the ellipse (for m=2\begin{document}$m=2$\end{document})ℰ⁢(i)={u∈ℝ2:u⊤⁢G⁢(i)⁢u=1},\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{E}(i)\;=\;\{\,u\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\;u^{\top}G(i)\,u=1\,\},$$\end{document}

whose principal axes have directions given by the columns of Qi\begin{document}$Q_{i}$\end{document} and semi-axis lengthsai=λi,1,bi=λi,2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle a_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i,1}},\qquad b_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i,2}}.$$\end{document}

Thus ai/bi=λi,1/λi,2\begin{document}$a_{i}/b_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i,1}/\lambda_{i,2}}$\end{document} quantifies local anisotropy (directional stretching), while detG(i)=λi,1λi,2\begin{document}$\det G(i)=\lambda_{i,1}\lambda_{i,2}$\end{document} quantifies local area change. In plots, we scale (ai,bi)\begin{document}$(a_{i},b_{i})$\end{document} by a global factor and ensure each ellipse fits within the axes (conservative circumscribed-circle bound) to avoid clipping.

sec.title: Contraction/expansion scalar field
sec.p: We color points (or ellipses) by a centered log-determinant of the metric,Def⁢(i)=log⁢det⁡G⁢(i)-center⁢({log⁢det⁡G⁢(j)}j=1N),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathrm{Def}(i)\;=\;\log\det G(i)\;-\;\mathrm{center}\big{(}\{\log\det G(j)\}_ {j=1}^{N}\big{)},$$\end{document}

with the center chosen as the median (robust) or mean, so that Def>0\begin{document}$\mathrm{Def} \gt 0$\end{document} indicates local expansion and Def<0\begin{document}$\mathrm{Def} \lt 0$\end{document} indicates contraction. Optionally, we smooth this scalar over the graph by t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} steps of diffusion, Def←PtDef\begin{document}$\mathrm{Def}\leftarrow P^{\,t}\mathrm{Def}$\end{document}, where P=D−1W\begin{document}$P=D^{-1}W$\end{document} is the random-walk operator derived from L=D−W\begin{document}$L=D-W$\end{document}; we then re-center and use robust percentile clipping with symmetric limits for color normalization.

sec.title: Visualization modes
sec.p: (i) Localized indicatrices: draw ellipses E(i)\begin{document}$\mathcal{E}(i)$\end{document} for a uniform subset of points, optionally modulating their size by a normalized anisotropy score log⁡(λi,1/λi,2)\begin{document}$\log(\lambda_{i,1}/\lambda_{i,2})$\end{document}. The underlying scatter may be colored by Def(i)\begin{document}$\mathrm{Def}(i)$\end{document} or other annotations. (ii) Grid-averaged field: build a regular grid over the embedding, and at each grid site g\begin{document}$g$\end{document} average nearby metrics,Gavg(g)=1k∑i∈Nk(g)G(i)\begin{document}$G_{\mathrm{avg}}(g)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(g)}G(i)$\end{document}; draw one ellipse from Gavg(g)\begin{document}$G_{\mathrm{avg}}(g)$\end{document} and color it by the grid-averaged Def\begin{document}$\mathrm{Def}$\end{document}. A thinning step enforces a minimum separation between grid sites to limit overlap.

sec.title: Geometric interpretation
sec.p: If ϕ:M→Rm\begin{document}$\phi:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}$\end{document} denotes the embedding map, then G(i)\begin{document}$G(i)$\end{document} estimates the pullback metric (dϕxi)⊤dϕxi\begin{document}$(\mathrm{d}\phi_{x_{i}})^{\top}\mathrm{d}\phi_{x_{i}}$\end{document} at xi\begin{document}$x_{i}$\end{document} (up to the discrete Laplacian normalization), so that log⁡detG(i)≈log⁡det((dϕxi)⊤dϕxi)\begin{document}$\log\det G(i)\approx\log\det\big{(}(\mathrm{d}\phi_{x_{i}})^{\top}\mathrm{d} \phi_{x_{i}}\big{)}$\end{document} reports local area change, and the eigenstructure of G(i)\begin{document}$G(i)$\end{document} reports directional distortion. The plotted indicatrices therefore act as distortion rulers, revealing where a 2-D layout expands, contracts, or shears the intrinsic geometry.

sec.title: Data imputation
sec.p: We perform diffusion-based imputation on the cell–cell graph. Let X∈RN×G\begin{document}$X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times G}$\end{document} denote the cell-by-gene matrix to be imputed, and let P∈RN×N\begin{document}$P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$\end{document} be the Markov (row-stochastic) diffusion operator built on the refined manifold graph. For a diffusion time t∈N\begin{document}$t\in\mathbb{N}$\end{document}, the imputed matrix is the graph diffusionX(t)=Pt⁢X,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle X^{(t)}\;=\;P^{\,t}\,X,$$\end{document}
that is each gene is smoothed across the graph while preserving its marginal scale.

sec.title: Automatic selection of the diffusion time
sec.p: To avoid oversmoothing, we select t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} from a candidate grid T={t1,…,tm}\begin{document}$\mathcal{T}=\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}\}$\end{document} by contrasting the gene–gene correlation structure of X(t)\begin{document}$X^{(t)}$\end{document} against a null in which cross-cell associations have been destroyed, but univariate marginals are preserved. Concretely, we first identify a small panel of HVGs to score. Let Xtop∈RN×g\begin{document}$X_{\mathrm{top}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times g}$\end{document} be the submatrix of these genes. For each t∈T\begin{document}$t\in\mathcal{T}$\end{document}:Xtop(t)=Pt⁢Xtop,C(t)=corr⁡(Xtop(t))∈ℝg×g,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle X_{\mathrm{top}}^{(t)}\;=\;P^{\,t}\,X_{\mathrm{top}},\qquad C^{(t)}\;=\; \operatorname{corr}\!\big{(}X_{\mathrm{top}}^{(t)}\big{)}\in\mathbb{R}^{g \times g},$$\end{document}

and we define a scalar score as the mean absolute off-diagonal correlation,Sobs⁢(t)=1g⁢(g-1)⁢∑a≠b|Ca⁢b(t)|.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{obs}}(t)\;=\;\frac{1}{g(g-1)}\sum_{a\neq b}\big{|}C^{(t)}_{ab}\big{ |}.$$\end{document}

sec.title: Null model and empirical test
sec.p: For each t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}, we generate a null distribution by independently permuting the rows of every column of Xtop\begin{document}$X_{\mathrm{top}}$\end{document} (gene-wise shuffling across cells), diffusing with the same t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}, and recomputing the score:for b=1,…,K: X~top(b)←row-permute(Xtop);X~top(b,t)=PtX~top(b);Snull(b)(t)=1g⁢(g-1)∑a≠b|corr(X~top(b,t))a⁢b|.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{for }b=1,\dots,K:\quad\widetilde{X}^{(b)}_{\mathrm{top}}\;\leftarrow\; \text{row-permute}(X_{\mathrm{top}})\,;\quad\widetilde{X}^{(b,t)}_{\mathrm{top }}\;=\;P^{\,t}\,\widetilde{X}^{(b)}_{\mathrm{top}}\,;\quad S_{\mathrm{null}}^{ (b)}(t)\;=\;\frac{1}{g(g-1)}\!\sum_{a\neq b}\big{|}\operatorname{corr}\big{(} \widetilde{X}^{(b,t)}_{\mathrm{top}}\big{)}_{ab}\big{|}.$$\end{document}

We then compute an empirical p\begin{document}$p$\end{document}-value and a z\begin{document}$z$\end{document}-score:pemp⁢(t)=1+#⁢{b:Snull(b)⁢(t)≥Sobs⁢(t)}1+K,z⁢(t)=Sobs⁢(t)-μnull⁢(t)σnull⁢(t)+10-9,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{emp}}(t)\;=\;\frac{1+\#\{\,b:\,S_{\mathrm{null}}^{(b)}(t)\geq S_{ \mathrm{obs}}(t)\,\}}{1+K},\qquad z(t)\;=\;\frac{S_{\mathrm{obs}}(t)-\mu_{ \mathrm{null}}(t)}{\sigma_{\mathrm{null}}(t)+10^{-9}},$$\end{document}

with μnull,σnull\begin{document}$\mu_{\mathrm{null}},\sigma_{\mathrm{null}}$\end{document} the mean and SD of {Snull(b)(t)}b=1K\begin{document}$\{S_{\mathrm{null}}^{(b)}(t)\}_{b=1}^{K}$\end{document}. The selected time ist⋆=arg⁡mint∈𝒯⁡pemp⁢(t) (tie-break by largest ⁢z⁢(t)⁢).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle t^{\star}\;=\;\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\,p_{\mathrm{emp}}(t)\quad\text{(tie- break by largest }z(t)\text{)}.$$\end{document}
After identifying an optimal diffusion time t, the optimal imputation result is:Ximp=Pt⋆⁢X .\begin{document}$$\displaystyle X_{\mathrm{imp}}\;=\;P^{\,t^{\star}}X\quad.$$\end{document}

This procedure selects the weakest amount of smoothing that yields gene–gene correlation structure significantly exceeding what diffusion would induce under a null with broken cross-cell associations. In doing so, it explicitly guards against the common pitfall of oversmoothing, where excessive diffusion can erase genuine biological heterogeneity and introduce spurious correlations that mimic structure but are in fact artifacts. By benchmarking the observed correlation profiles against an empirical null, the method ensures that only structure reproducibly supported by the data is retained. This design minimizes the risk of false positives: correlations that arise purely from graph connectivity rather than underlying transcriptional programs are filtered out, since they also appear in the null distribution and therefore fail the statistical test. At the same time, genuine patterns of co-expression that reflect biological coordination between genes are amplified, as they persist in the observed data but not under randomized permutations. The approach thus balances denoising with fidelity to the original data, producing imputations that are statistically principled, biologically meaningful, and less likely to bias downstream analyses such as clustering, trajectory inference, or differential expression.

sec.title: Signal filtering
sec.p: TopoMetry provides a graph-based low-pass filter to denoise sample-level signals while respecting manifold structure. Let s∈RN\begin{document}$s\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$\end{document} be a per-cell signal and P∈RN×N\begin{document}$P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$\end{document} the row-stochastic diffusion operator on the refined graph (default: built in the multiscale spectral scaffold space). The filtered signal after t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} diffusion steps iss(t)=Pt⁢s,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s^{(t)}\;=\;P^{\,t}\,s,$$\end{document}

which corresponds to heat-kernel smoothing on the graph: increasing t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} attenuates high-frequency (noisy, rapidly varying) components and preserves low-frequency structure aligned with the topology.

sec.title: Signal construction
sec.p: Users supply a column in the sample annotations. If the column is categorical, we form a binary indicatorsi= 1⁢{cell ⁢i⁢ belongs to the category of interest},\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{i}\;=\;\mathbf{1}\{\,\text{cell }i\text{ belongs to the category of interest}\,\},$$\end{document}

else a numeric column is used directly (non-finite entries set to 0). For stress tests, one may optionally add pre-filter Gaussian noise, s←s+σε\begin{document}$s\leftarrow s+\sigma\varepsilon$\end{document} with ε∼N(0,I)\begin{document}$\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$\end{document} and σ≥0\begin{document}$\sigma\geq 0$\end{document}.

sec.title: Choice of operator and time
sec.p: Filtering can use the Markov operator derived in any space (msZ,Z,X\begin{document}$\texttt{msZ},\texttt{Z},\texttt{X}$\end{document}); the default msZ leverages the refined multiscale geometry. The parameter t∈N\begin{document}$t\in\mathbb{N}$\end{document} controls smoothness: t=0\begin{document}$t=0$\end{document} returns the original signal, small t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} mildly denoises within neighborhoods, and large t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} approaches the stationary distribution (oversmoothing). In practice, modest values (e.g. t≈4−8\begin{document}$t\approx 4\!-\!8$\end{document}) preserve biological contrasts while reducing noise.

sec.title: Normalization (optional)
sec.p: After filtering, an optional rescaling can be applied. If the signal is intended as a probability or indicator, one can keep the native range. Otherwise, a min–max normalization maps s(t)\begin{document}$s^{(t)}$\end{document} to [0, 1]:s^(t)=s(t)-mini⁡si(t)maxi⁡si(t)-mini⁡si(t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \widehat{s}^{(t)}\;=\;\frac{s^{(t)}-\min_{i}s^{(t)}_{i}}{\max_{i}s^{(t)}_{i}- \min_{i}s^{(t)}_{i}}\,,$$\end{document}
guarded for degenerate ranges. This facilitates downstream visualization and thresholding.

For reproducibility, both the raw vector and its filtered counterpart are recorded in the sample metadata, including the diffusion time t\begin{document}$t$\end{document} and the operator choice. The procedure is computationally light (matrix–vector products, compatible with sparse P\begin{document}$P$\end{document}) and can be applied to categorical labels, risk scores, or any continuous per-cell quantity to obtain geometry-aware smoothed estimates.

sec.title: Quantification of geometry preservation
sec.p: To systematically evaluate how well different representations preserve the intrinsic geometry of single-cell data, we developed a set of four complementary metrics. Each metric operates directly on the diffusion operators associated with the original data space and the candidate embedding, thereby enabling a scale-aware and operator-native assessment of geometry preservation.

sec.title: Row-neighborhood F1 score (PF1)
sec.p: Let Px\begin{document}$P_{x}$\end{document} and Py\begin{document}$P_{y}$\end{document} denote two row-stochastic diffusion operators to be compared. For each cell i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, let Nx(i)\begin{document}$N_{x}(i)$\end{document} and Ny(i)\begin{document}$N_{y}(i)$\end{document} denote the sets of the top-k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} neighbors defined by the largest transition probabilities in Px\begin{document}$P_{x}$\end{document} and Py\begin{document}$P_{y}$\end{document}, respectively. The per-row F1 score is given byF1⁢(i)=2⁢|Nx⁢(i)∩Ny⁢(i)||Nx⁢(i)|+|Ny⁢(i)|,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{F1}(i)\;=\;\frac{2\,|N_{x}(i)\cap N_{y}(i)|}{|N_{x}(i)|+|N_{y}(i)|},$$\end{document}
and the PF1 score is obtained as the average over all cells:PF1=1n⁢∑i=1nF1⁢(i).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{PF1}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{F1}(i).$$\end{document}
This score captures the preservation of local neighborhood identities, independently of edge weights.

sec.title: Row-wise Jensen–Shannon similarity (PJS)
sec.p: To compare the transition probability distributions themselves, we use the JS divergence. For each row i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, let pi\begin{document}$p_{i}$\end{document} and qi\begin{document}$q_{i}$\end{document} denote the probability vectors corresponding to the nonzero transitions of Px\begin{document}$P_{x}$\end{document} and Py\begin{document}$P_{y}$\end{document}. The JS divergence between pi\begin{document}$p_{i}$\end{document} and qi\begin{document}$q_{i}$\end{document} isJS⁢(pi,qi)=12⁢KL⁢(pi∥mi)+12⁢KL⁢(qi∥mi),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{JS}(p_{i},q_{i})=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{KL}\!\left(p_{i}\,\Big{\|}\,m_{i} \right)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{KL}\!\left(q_{i}\,\Big{\|}\,m_{i}\right),$$\end{document}

where mi=12(pi+qi)\begin{document}$m_{i}=\tfrac{1}{2}(p_{i}+q_{i})$\end{document} and KL denotes the Kullback–Leibler divergence. We then define the similarity asPJS=1-1n⁢∑i=1nJS⁢(pi,qi).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{PJS}=1-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{JS}(p_{i},q_{i}).$$\end{document}
Unlike PF1, this metric is sensitive to the weights of transitions, thus evaluating the fidelity of local transition probabilities.

sec.title: Spectral procrustes alignment (SP)
sec.p: Diffusion operators admit an eigendecomposition Pψℓ=λℓψℓ\begin{document}$P\psi_{\ell}=\lambda_{\ell}\psi_{\ell}$\end{document}, where {λℓ,ψℓ}\begin{document}$\{\lambda_{\ell},\psi_{\ell}\}$\end{document} are eigenpairs ordered by |λℓ|\begin{document}$|\lambda_{\ell}|$\end{document}. For a given timescale t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}, the diffusion map is defined asΦt⁢(i)=(λ1t⁢ψ1⁢(i),…,λrt⁢ψr⁢(i)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Phi_{t}(i)=\left(\lambda_{1}^{t}\psi_{1}(i),\ldots,\lambda_{r}^{t}\psi_{r}(i) \right).$$\end{document}

Given the diffusion coordinates Φtx\begin{document}$\Phi_{t}^{x}$\end{document} and Φty\begin{document}$\Phi_{t}^{y}$\end{document} from Px\begin{document}$P_{x}$\end{document} and Py\begin{document}$P_{y}$\end{document}, we align them via orthogonal Procrustes:R*=arg⁡minR⊤⁢R=I⁡∥Φty⁢R-Φtx∥F2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle R^{*}=\arg\min_{R^{\top}R=I}\|\Phi_{t}^{y}R-\Phi_{t}^{x}\|_{F}^{2}.$$\end{document}

The alignment quality is quantified by the coefficient of determination,R2=1-∥Φtx-Φty⁢R*∥F2∥Φtx∥F2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle R^{2}=1-\frac{\|\Phi_{t}^{x}-\Phi_{t}^{y}R^{*}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\Phi_{t}^{x}\|_{F} ^{2}}.$$\end{document}
The SP score is averaged across multiple diffusion times t\begin{document}$t$\end{document}, capturing agreement of the meso- and global-scale geometry of the manifold.

sec.title: Rationale for metric selection
sec.p: These three metrics together capture complementary aspects of geometry preservation across scales: PF1 and PJS quantify fidelity of local neighborhoods, and SP evaluates alignment of diffusion eigencoordinates at mesoscopic scales. Compared to previously used metrics, they provide a more faithful evaluation of single-cell representations. Global scores based on PCA depend strongly on graph-layout initialization rather than underlying geometry. Geodesic correlation, though sensitive to structure, overweights large-scale distances and becomes biased in the presence of multiple disjoint submanifolds, as typical in single-cell data. Clustering- or label-based scores are unreliable in real-world settings where ground-truth identities are unknown. Finally, Riemannian diagnostics such as distortion heatmaps and indicatrices are restricted to 2-D embeddings, whereas single-cell analyses require latent spaces with tens or hundreds of dimensions. Our operator-native metrics therefore offer a principled, scalable, and interpretable quantification of geometry preservation across learned representations.

sec.title: Standard analysis workflow
sec.p: Single-cell analysis workflows have converged on a widely adopted pipeline that couples dimensionality reduction by PCA with graph construction and visualization using UMAP. This approach underpins the majority of published studies and is implemented as the default in most software ecosystems for single-cell genomics.

sec.title: Preprocessing
sec.p: Raw count matrices are typically subjected to two standard preprocessing steps. First, counts are normalized for library size (total molecules per cell) and log-transformed to stabilize variance. Second, a subset of HVGs is selected, usually between 1000 and 5000, under the assumption that these capture the majority of biologically relevant variation while reducing technical noise. The resulting HVG matrix is then standardized (Z-score normalized) so that each gene has mean zero and unit variance, preventing highly expressed genes from dominating subsequent analyses.

sec.title: Principal component analysis
sec.p: The standardized HVG matrix is projected into a lower-dimensional space using PCA. The number of retained components is typically chosen heuristically (e.g. 30–100) based on an ad hoc ‘elbow point’, rather than based on intrinsic dimensionality. The Euclidean distances between cells in this PCA space are then used to build a k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}-nearest-neighbors (kNN) graph, which serves as the foundation for clustering and visualization.

sec.title: UMAP graph layout
sec.p: The kNN graph is converted into an affinity graph using fuzzy simplicial sets, which UMAP optimizes into a two-dimensional embedding. The resulting map aims to preserve local neighborhoods while maintaining a global structure that is visually interpretable. This 2-D representation is widely used for cluster annotation, lineage inference, and exploratory analysis, despite being optimized for visualization rather than strict geometric fidelity.

sec.title: Clustering and identification of marker genes
sec.p: Clustering was performed with the Leiden community detection algorithm using default parameters via scanpy.tl.leiden. To ensure fair comparisons, we applied the same clustering algorithm with identical resolution parameters across all evaluated workflows, including TopoMetry. Marker genes were identified with scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups after constructing dendrograms on the representation associated with the clustering results, using the logistic regression method (method=’logreg’), which has been shown to achieve optimal results in single-cell data (Ntranos et al., 2019).

sec.title: Summary
sec.p: Together, these steps—log and size normalization, HVG selection, Z-score standardization, PCA projection, kNN graph construction, and UMAP embedding—constitute the de facto standard in single-cell analysis. While computationally efficient and easy to implement, the workflow is based on strong assumptions: that global variance identifies biologically meaningful structure, that a fixed number of PCs captures the latent geometry, and that UMAP embeddings accurately reflect manifold relationships. These assumptions have rarely been tested systematically, motivating the development of alternative frameworks such as TopoMetry.

sec.title: RNA velocity analysis
sec.p: RNA velocity analysis was performed using the scVelo toolkit (Bergen et al., 2020), with all steps executed using default parameters. The exception was the calculation of neighborhood graphs and moments, which by default rely on the PCA latent space, but were instead computed using the TopoMetry multiscale spectral scaffold. For TopoMetry analysis, spliced and unspliced counts were aggregated, and default preprocessing was applied to provide a standardized matrix of gene expression as input.

sec.title: T cell receptor analysis
sec.p: The ECCITE-TCR dataset was obtained with precomputed TCR analysis and metadata. For the TICA dataset, TCR clonotype analysis was performed using the scirpy toolkit for immune receptor analysis in Python (Sturm et al., 2020). TCR similarities were computed using the alignment of amino acid sequences. Default parameters were used for all remaining steps.

sec.title: Variational inference
sec.p: Variational autoencoder analyses were performed using the scvi-tools framework (Lopez et al., 2018; Gayoso et al., 2022). Models were trained on GPU using default parameters, including preprocessing steps handled internally by the package. Latent spaces were computed and used to construct neighborhood graphs for Leiden clustering and UMAP visualizations.

sec.title: Public datasets
sec.p: We assembled a corpus of publicly available single-cell RNA-seq collections from the CellxGene Census (release 2023-07-25). For each target collection_id, we queried the Census metadata table (census_info/datasets) to obtain the corresponding dataset_ids and then retrieved primary RNA measurements (is_primary_data = True) as AnnData objects separately for Homo sapiens and Mus musculus. Observational annotations included tissue-level fields (e.g. tissue, tissue_general, assay, cell_type). Individual datasets within a collection were concatenated (outer join) after loading. To ensure basic quality, we removed cells with fewer than 100 detected genes and genes expressed in fewer than five cells prior to downstream analysis. For computational tractability, collections with more than 105 cells were excluded from this benchmarking pass, as were a small number of collections exhibiting upstream data issues (e.g. malformed or inconsistent matrices). For each processed collection we stored a compact result bundle containing: collection identifiers and names, cell and gene counts, a set of two-dimensional embeddings, and a results blob with evaluation tables and diagnostics. Additional datasets analyzed in this manuscript are also publicly available: The murine pancreas development dataset was obtained through the scVelo toolkit for RNA velocity estimation and visualization. The PBMC68k dataset was freely downloaded from 10 X Genomics. Additional PBMC datasets were obtained from the accession codes phs002048.v1.p1 (LES), GSE154386 (Dengue), and GSE138266 (MS). The paired RNA and TCR datasets were made publicly available by their authors and were obtained from Zenodo and from the Human Cell Atlas.

sec.title: Performance benchmark
sec.p: All methods were applied to the same preprocessed matrices (HVGs, library-size normalization, log⁡(1+x)\begin{document}$\log(1{+}x)$\end{document}, scaling), as described in the preceding section. We evaluated geometry-preservation performance across representations using a unified routine that computes neighborhood- and diffusion-based scores.
Concretely, for each collection:

list-item.p: We computed a standard PCA model (up to 200 components or the maximal feasible given ncells\begin{document}$n_{\text{cells}}$\end{document} and ngenes\begin{document}$n_{\text{genes}}$\end{document}) and retained:
UMAP computed directly on the scaled expression space with cosine distance (X_UMAP_on_X).
We trained an SCVI model on raw counts (default scvi-tools settings), extracted the latent representation (X_scVI), and computed UMAP on its neighborhood graph (X_UMAP_on_scVI).

We ran TopoMetry via tp.sc.fit_adata, which builds a first kernel on expression, performs an eigendecomposition to obtain a spectral scaffold, and refines the kernel on that scaffold before producing low-dimensional projections (e.g. TopoMAP/TopoPaCMAP). The fitted TopOGraph exposes Markov operators PX\begin{document}$P_{X}$\end{document}, PZ\begin{document}$P_{Z}$\end{document}, and PmsZ\begin{document}$P_{\text{ms}Z}$\end{document} used in evaluation.

sec.p: We assessed geometry preservation for all representations present in adata.obsm using the same parameters: Euclidean distance, local neighborhood size k=30\begin{document}$k{=}30$\end{document}, HNSW-based approximate nearest-neighbors search, and diffusion times t∈{1,4,8}\begin{document}$t\in\{1,4,8\}$\end{document} with spectral rank r=64\begin{document}$r{=}64$\end{document}. The evaluation routine reports a table of metrics, including row-neighborhood k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}-NN overlap (PF1), row-wise JS similarity (PJS), and SP alignment. PCA diagnostics recorded per collection included the full variance-explained spectrum and its cumulative sum. Default hyperparameters were used for all evaluated workflows to enable a fair performance comparison across datasets.
